lessons.title: The Stresemann era — recovery and Weimar culture
lessons.description: New currency, Dawes and Young Plans, Locarno — were the Golden Years built on borrowed time?
lessons.content_html:
From the wreckage of November 1923 a different Germany emerged. By 1928 unemployment was below 1.4 million, foreign investment was flooding in, and Berlin was the cultural capital of Europe. Historians call the years 1924–1929 the ‘Golden Years’ or ‘Stresemann era’ after the Foreign Minister who steered the recovery. But how golden were they? The German historian Detlev Peukert argued Weimar was ‘dancing on a volcano’ — that the recovery was real but built on US loans that could be recalled at any moment. The 1929 Wall Street Crash would prove him right.

Stresemann: Pragmatist, Not Saviour

Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor in August 1923 at the height of hyperinflation. His chancellorship lasted only 100 days, but it was the most decisive 100 days in Weimar history. He called off passive resistance in the Ruhr in late September 1923, accepting that the strike could not be won. He then introduced the temporary new currency, the Rentenmark, in November 1923. One Rentenmark exchanged for one trillion old paper marks. The new currency was backed by a mortgage on land and industrial property, and Germans agreed to trust it.

In August 1924 the Rentenmark was replaced by the permanent Reichsmark, backed partly by gold reserves. Stresemann himself was pushed out as Chancellor in November 1923, but he then served as Foreign Minister in every government from 1923 until his death in 1929 — six years of continuity in a system famous for its instability.

Key Fact

The Rentenmark replaced the worthless paper mark in November 1923 (1 Rentenmark = 1 trillion old marks). It was itself replaced by the permanent Reichsmark in August 1924, ending hyperinflation. Stresemann then served as Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in 1929.

The Dawes Plan, 1924

Reparations remained the political wound that would not close. Stresemann's strategy was to admit Germany could not refuse them but argue it could not pay them at the 1921 schedule. American banker Charles Dawes was invited to chair an international commission. The Dawes Plan of August 1924 set graduated payments — smaller in early years, rising as Germany recovered — and crucially provided 800 million gold marks in American loans to kick-start the economy.

Over the next five years roughly 25 billion marks of US capital flowed into Germany. Industry rebuilt. Berlin's U-Bahn extended. New housing replaced wartime slums. Industrial output passed 1913 levels by 1928. By 1928 Germany was paying reparations broadly out of US loans — a circular flow that worked only as long as American money kept arriving.

Locarno, the League and the Young Plan

Stresemann's foreign policy aim was to ease Germany back into the European system as a respected partner, not a defeated outcast. In October 1925 he signed the Locarno Treaties, in which Germany voluntarily accepted its western borders with France and Belgium. Crucially the treaties left the eastern borders — with Poland and Czechoslovakia — open to future revision. To Germans this hinted that Versailles could be peacefully chipped at.

In September 1926 Germany was admitted to the League of Nations as a permanent member of its Council, equal in rank with Britain, France, Italy and Japan. In 1928 Germany signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact renouncing war as an instrument of policy — alongside fifteen other major powers.

The Young Plan of 1929, named after another American banker (Owen Young), reduced reparations from 132 billion gold marks to 112 billion and stretched payments to 1988. The political right hated it because it accepted reparations existed at all; right-wing parties including the small Nazi Party joined a referendum campaign against the plan in 1929. Their campaign lost — but it gave Hitler national exposure and respectable allies for the first time.

Examiner reports flag this confusion every series. The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured payments and brought in US loans — it did not reduce the total bill. The Young Plan (1929) actually cut the bill (from 132 to 112 billion) and stretched it to 1988. Dawes 1924 = restructure. Young 1929 = reduce. Memorise the pair as Dawes Restructure, Young Reduce.

Weimar Culture: Bauhaus, Brecht and Berlin Cabaret

As Germany stabilised politically, an extraordinary cultural flowering followed. Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus design school in 1919 — its modernist buildings, furniture and graphic design defined the era. Bertolt Brecht's plays (The Threepenny Opera, 1928) reinvented theatre. Berlin's cabarets, immortalised by Christopher Isherwood and later by the musical Cabaret, blended jazz, satire and sexual freedom unprecedented in European cities. The German film industry rivalled Hollywood: Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927) and the first synchronised-sound film The Blue Angel (1930) were international hits.

For modernists this was liberation. For conservatives, particularly in rural Germany and the Catholic south, it was a moral collapse — what the Nazis later called ‘cultural Bolshevism’. Even some Weimar supporters worried that Berlin's cabarets and the Bauhaus's flat-roofed houses had little in common with how most Germans actually lived.

Limits of the Recovery

For all the headlines, the ‘Golden Years’ were patchy. Unemployment never fell below 1.3 million. Agriculture was already in depression by 1927 as world grain prices collapsed; small farmers struggled with debts. The recovery depended on US loans that could be recalled at three months’ notice. Coalition governments remained short-lived: there were six Chancellors between 1923 and 1929. President Friedrich Ebert died in 1925 and was replaced by 78-year-old Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg — a war hero of the right who privately disliked the Republic he was now meant to defend.

Optimists like the historian Eberhard Kolb point to genuine industrial recovery, peace with neighbours, and democratic stability. Pessimists like Detlev Peukert argue the recovery was hollow — rural depression, dependence on US loans, an ageing right-wing President. The truth is mixed: Weimar genuinely recovered, but its recovery sat on foundations only as solid as the New York stock market. When Stresemann died on 3 October 1929, weeks before the Wall Street Crash, even contemporaries felt his death marked the end of the era. The streets of Berlin filled with mourners. Within five months of Wall Street's collapse, German unemployment doubled.

Key Fact

Stresemann's recovery rested on three pillars: a stable currency, US loans through the Dawes Plan, and diplomatic reintegration through Locarno and the League. All three were genuine achievements — but the second was beyond German control, which is why the 1929 Wall Street Crash hit Germany harder than any other major economy.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation question on the Stresemann era, watch for sources that simplify recovery as either complete (optimist view) or illusory (pessimist view). Top answers integrate both: real industrial growth and diplomatic gains alongside rural depression and dependence on US loans. Memorise three date pairs: Rentenmark Nov 1923 / Reichsmark Aug 1924; Dawes 1924 / Young 1929; Locarno Oct 1925 / League membership 1926. Don't confuse the Dawes Plan (restructured) with the Young Plan (reduced).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stresemann's Rentenmark of November 1923 ended hyperinflation; the Dawes Plan of 1924 restructured reparations and brought US loans worth roughly 25 billion marks over five years.
  • Locarno (1925), League membership (1926) and the Young Plan (1929) reintegrated Germany into European diplomacy — the right hated all three but the campaign against them gave Hitler new exposure.
  • Weimar culture flourished — Bauhaus, Brecht, Berlin cabaret — but the recovery was uneven (rural depression, persistent unemployment) and dependent on US loans that could be recalled at three months’ notice.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1928 SPD pamphlet praising the Stresemann era as a genuine recovery and democratic success) and Interpretation B (a 1989 academic study by Detlev Peukert arguing Weimar in 1924–29 was ‘dancing on a volcano’) on the Stresemann era. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Stresemann era as a real success — stable currency, falling unemployment, diplomatic recognition through Locarno and League membership.
• Interpretation B presents it as fragile — rural depression, dependence on US loans, persistent political instability under an ageing right-wing President.
• Main difference: A emphasises measurable gains; B emphasises hidden structural weaknesses.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1928 SPD pamphlet on the Stresemann era) and Interpretation B (a 1989 academic study by Peukert) give different views about the ‘Golden Years’.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the 1928 SPD pamphlet aimed to win the next election by promoting the SPD's role in stabilising the Republic; Peukert's 1989 study aimed at scholarly analysis of long-term outcomes.
• They use different evidence — the SPD pamphlet emphasised industrial output and Locarno; Peukert integrates rural debt, US loan dependence and the rise of the Nazis after 1929.
• They were produced at different times — the 1928 source had no knowledge of the Wall Street Crash; Peukert benefits from sixty years of hindsight.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Stresemann's foreign policy of voluntary cooperation with the Allies was the most important achievement of the Weimar Republic, paving the way for German reintegration into Europe.' How convincing is Interpretation A about Stresemann's foreign policy?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because Locarno (October 1925) saw Germany voluntarily accept its western borders, easing French fears and earning international goodwill.
• Convincing because the League of Nations admitted Germany as a permanent Council member in 1926, restoring great-power status only seven years after Versailles.
• Less convincing because Locarno deliberately left the eastern borders open to revision, hinting that Stresemann's diplomacy was tactical rather than purely cooperative.
• Less convincing because the right rejected reintegration outright — the 1929 referendum against the Young Plan gave Hitler national exposure and previewed the Nazi threat.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing for Western diplomacy, but the eastern question and right-wing backlash limit the achievement.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

You may consider:

practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Currency reform: the Rentenmark of November 1923 ended hyperinflation; the permanent Reichsmark followed in August 1924. • Dawes Plan (1924): restructured reparations; provided 800 million gold marks in US loans; roughly 25 billion marks of US capital flowed into Germany over five years; industrial output passed 1913 levels by 1928. • Diplomatic recovery: Locarno (1925) accepted western borders; League membership (1926); Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928); Young Plan (1929) reduced and stretched reparations. • Weimar culture: Bauhaus, Bertolt Brecht's plays, Berlin cabaret, Fritz Lang's Metropolis; but conservative backlash also growing. • Limits of recovery: unemployment never below 1.3 million; rural depression from 1927; six Chancellors between 1923 and 1929; Hindenburg replaced Ebert in 1925. • Conclusion: recovery was real but partial — economic and diplomatic gains rested on US loans and a fragile coalition; when Wall Street collapsed in October 1929 the foundations gave way. [Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1929 right-wing nationalist pamphlet attacking the Young Plan as a betrayal of Germany) and Interpretation B (a 1929 SPD newspaper editorial defending the Young Plan as a major reduction of reparations) on the Young Plan. What is the main difference between these views?

Students may include:

• Interpretation B defends the Young Plan as success — it cut total reparations from 132 to 112 billion gold marks and gave Germany a clear path out of debt.

[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The cultural energy of Weimar Germany — Bauhaus, Brecht, Berlin cabaret — was disconnected from the rest of the country, and its very brilliance fuelled conservative backlash.' How convincing is Interpretation A about Weimar culture?
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Convincing because the cultural revival was concentrated in Berlin and a few cities — Bauhaus headquarters, Brecht's theatre, jazz cabarets — while small towns and rural Germany had little exposure. • Convincing because conservatives, the churches and rural voters were genuinely alarmed by what they saw as moral collapse, providing rhetorical material the Nazis would later use to attack ‘cultural Bolshevism’. • Less convincing because Weimar culture had a wide reach in some areas — the German film industry exported globally; Metropolis (1927) and The Blue Angel (1930) were popular hits. • Less convincing because the conservative backlash had many sources, not just culture — agrarian depression, fear of communism and Versailles resentment all fed the right's growth. • Overall judgement: convincing for the urban-rural split and conservative backlash, but oversimplifies the cultural reach. [Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

lessons.title: The Depression and the rise of the Nazis, 1928-1932
lessons.description: How a Wall Street crash 5,000 miles away put Hitler within reach of power.
lessons.content_html:
In May 1928, three months before the Wall Street Crash, the Nazi Party polled 2.6% in the Reichstag election. By July 1932 it polled 37.4% and was the largest party in Germany. Nothing about the Nazi programme had changed in those four years — what changed was the world economy. The Great Depression handed Hitler the votes that the Munich Putsch had failed to seize by force. Examiner reports flag this every series: it was the Depression that caused Hitler's rise, not the other way around. Direction of causation matters.

The Wall Street Crash, October 1929

On 24 October 1929 (‘Black Thursday’) the New York Stock Exchange collapsed. By the following Tuesday share prices had lost a quarter of their value. American banks called in their international loans — including those that had funded German industry under the Dawes Plan. Germany had borrowed roughly 25 billion marks of US capital between 1924 and 1929. Almost overnight that flow reversed.

The result was the deepest economic collapse Germany had ever experienced. Industrial production fell by 40% between 1929 and 1932. Banks failed. By 1932 over six million Germans were unemployed — about a third of the workforce. Many more were on short-time work. Soup queues stretched through major cities. Young men in particular saw no prospect of work; many drifted into Communist or Nazi paramilitary units which offered uniforms, food and a sense of purpose.

Key Fact

The Nazi Party rose from 12 Reichstag seats in 1928 to 230 seats in July 1932 — a thirteenfold rise in four years. The cause was the Depression, not Nazi policy: the party's programme had not changed. Nazi support actually fell to 196 seats in November 1932, showing the surge was unstable.

Bruning and the Politics of Austerity

In March 1930 the SPD-led grand coalition collapsed over how to fund unemployment insurance. President Hindenburg appointed the Centre Party's Heinrich Bruning. Bruning had no Reichstag majority. Instead Hindenburg used Article 48 of the constitution to let him rule by emergency decree. Five separate emergency decrees passed in 1931 alone. Bruning's policy was deflation: cut wages, cut benefits, cut government spending. He believed this would force prices down, restore competitiveness and let Germany trade its way out.

It made the Depression worse. Cutting benefits when six million were unemployed simply meant more starvation and more political extremism. Bruning was nicknamed the ‘Hunger Chancellor’. By 1932 the use of Article 48 had become routine: Hindenburg passed 66 emergency decrees compared to only five Reichstag laws. Weimar parliamentary democracy was effectively dead before Hitler ever became Chancellor.

Hindenburg was 84 by 1932 and surrounded by a small camarilla of right-wing advisers including his son Oskar and General Kurt von Schleicher. They saw the Depression as an opportunity to build an authoritarian government that bypassed the SPD altogether. Article 48 had been designed as an emergency safety valve in 1919; under Hindenburg it became a routine governing tool. This was the political space the Nazis would exploit: a President willing to govern without parliament, a Chancellor pursuing austerity that immiserated millions, and a Reichstag that no longer functioned.

The Nazi Surge, 1930–1932

In the September 1930 Reichstag election the Nazi vote leapt from 2.6% to 18.3%. The party won 107 seats, becoming the second-largest party. The Communists (KPD) also doubled their vote, reaching 13.1%. Together the two extreme parties controlled almost a third of the Reichstag. The political centre — SPD, Centre, liberals — was being squeezed from both sides.

In April 1932 Hitler stood for President against Hindenburg. He lost, but won 36% of the vote in the second round — not bad for a man who had only become a German citizen in February 1932. In July 1932 Reichstag elections he polled 37.4% and won 230 seats, becoming the largest single party. By this point the Nazi vote had grown thirteenfold in four years. But it had not grown enough: the Nazis still needed coalition partners or a presidential appointment to take power.

The Role of the SA

The Nazi vote was secured on the streets as well as at the ballot box. The SA (Sturmabteilung), led by Ernst Röhm after his return from Bolivia in 1930, grew from around 100,000 in 1930 to roughly 400,000 by July 1932 — larger than the Reichswehr army. SA ‘brownshirts’ broke up Communist and SPD meetings, marched in uniformed columns through working-class districts, and provided street muscle at every Nazi rally.

Crucially, the SA also offered welfare the state had stopped providing. Soup kitchens, dormitories, free uniforms and a sense of belonging drew unemployed young men in. By 1932 over half the SA was unemployed. Street violence escalated: in the summer of 1932 alone around 100 people were killed in Nazi–Communist clashes. To frightened middle-class voters this looked like civil war — and the Nazis successfully painted themselves as the only force capable of restoring order.

Hitler offered different things to different audiences, held together by Joseph Goebbels's modern propaganda machine. To the unemployed: jobs, food, dignity, work creation. To the middle class: protection from Communism, restoration of order, recovery of lost savings. To farmers: subsidies and protectionism against cheap imports. To industrialists: an end to trade-union militancy and a commitment to rearmament. To nationalists: revision of Versailles. To everyone: Volksgemeinschaft, a unified national community transcending class. Goebbels's posters, films and modern aircraft tours (Hitler flew to twenty cities in five days during the 1932 campaign) reached audiences other parties could not.

November 1932: The Vote Falls

In November 1932 fresh elections were called. The Nazi vote fell from 37.4% to 33.1% — from 230 seats to 196. Party finances were desperate. Goebbels's diary recorded morale collapsing. The KPD vote rose by another two percentage points. If parliamentary politics had simply continued, the Nazi surge might have run out of steam. But by November 1932 parliamentary politics had ceased to function. Hindenburg's small circle of advisers were already negotiating a way to bring Hitler into a controlled cabinet. The Depression had not fixed itself; it had broken the political system in which moderates might have survived.

Key Fact

The Communist KPD also grew rapidly during the Depression — from 10.6% in 1928 to 16.9% in November 1932. Many middle-class Germans voted Nazi not from love of Hitler but from fear of a Bolshevik revolution. Bruning's austerity, the SA's street violence and the KPD's rise together convinced enough voters that only an authoritarian regime could restore order.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Two examiner trip-wires for this lesson. First, do not write that Hitler caused the Depression — the Depression caused Hitler's rise. Direction of causation matters and gets flagged every series. Second, do not assume the Nazis were always popular. They polled only 2.6% in 1928 and their vote actually fell from 37% to 33% between July and November 1932. For the 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation question, watch for sources that overstate Hitler's appeal as the cause of his rise, when fear of Communism, Bruning's austerity and the SA's street violence all mattered too. Lock in the seat totals: 12 (1928), 107 (1930), 230 (July 1932), 196 (Nov 1932).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1929 Wall Street Crash recalled US loans to Germany, triggering a 40% fall in industrial output and six million unemployed by 1932 — this was the cause of the Nazi surge, not Nazi policy.
  • Bruning's deflationary austerity from 1930 worsened the Depression and replaced parliamentary government with rule by Article 48 emergency decree, hollowing out Weimar democracy before Hitler took power.
  • Hitler's appeal combined targeted promises (jobs, order, anti-Communism, anti-Versailles) with mass propaganda and SA street violence — but Nazi support peaked at 37.4% in July 1932 and fell back in November, showing the surge was unstable.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1932 Nazi Party leaflet claiming Hitler offered the only solution to mass unemployment) and Interpretation B (a 1932 SPD newspaper editorial blaming Bruning's austerity for the depth of the Depression) on the cause of the political crisis of 1930–32. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the crisis as solvable only by Hitler — mass unemployment, dependency on US loans and political stalemate required a strong leader.
• Interpretation B presents the crisis as worsened by Bruning's deflationary policies — cuts to wages and benefits when six million were unemployed deepened the slump.
• Main difference: A frames the crisis as a leadership vacuum requiring Hitler; B frames it as policy failure that created political space for extremism.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1932 Nazi leaflet) and Interpretation B (a 1932 SPD newspaper editorial) give different views about the cause of the 1930–32 political crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the Nazi leaflet aimed to recruit voters frightened by unemployment; the SPD editorial aimed to defend the elected government against authoritarianism.
• They use different evidence — the leaflet cites unemployment figures and Hitler's leadership claims; the editorial cites Bruning's emergency decrees and Article 48 abuse.
• They were produced from different political positions — both written in 1932 but with opposing interests in how the crisis was interpreted.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The 1929 Wall Street Crash and the Depression that followed were the single most important cause of Hitler's rise to power.' How convincing is Interpretation A about the rise of the Nazi Party between 1928 and 1932?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (12 seats) in 1928 to 37.4% (230 seats) in July 1932 — a thirteenfold rise that exactly tracked unemployment reaching six million.
• Convincing because Nazi policy did not change in this period — the surge was driven by external economic catastrophe, not by ideological conversion.
• Less convincing because Bruning's austerity worsened the Depression and made the political system uniquely vulnerable — a different Chancellor might have contained the Nazi rise.
• Less convincing because Nazi propaganda, SA street violence and fear of Communism all contributed; the Depression was the trigger but not the only cause.
• Less convincing because Nazi support actually fell from 37% to 33% by November 1932, suggesting the Depression alone was not driving an unstoppable rise.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing as the trigger but understates the role of Bruning, propaganda and political miscalculation by Hindenburg's circle.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

lessons.title: The failure of Weimar democracy and Hitler's appointment
lessons.description: Backstairs deals, election results and the day Hindenburg handed the keys to Hitler.
lessons.content_html:
By the end of 1932 the Nazi vote was falling and the party was almost bankrupt. Yet on 30 January 1933 Adolf Hitler walked into the Reich Chancellery as the new Chancellor of Germany. The puzzle of this lesson is how a party that had just lost 34 Reichstag seats in November came to power eight weeks later. The answer is not that Hitler was ‘voted in’ — the Nazis never won an outright majority in a free election. He was appointed by an 85-year-old President after a sequence of backstairs deals between elite conservatives who believed they could control him.

The April 1932 Presidential Election

The crisis of 1932 began with the presidential election. Paul von Hindenburg, then 84, stood for re-election against Hitler. Hindenburg won the second round in April 1932 with 53% to Hitler's 36%, but the result shook the conservative establishment. Hitler had won 13 million votes and proved that the Nazi movement was a permanent feature of German politics.

Hindenburg disliked Hitler personally — he called him ‘the Bohemian corporal’ — but the President was now surrounded by a small group of right-wing advisers including his son Oskar and General Kurt von Schleicher. They concluded that the only way to govern without the SPD was to harness the Nazi vote inside a controlled cabinet.

Key Fact

Germany had four chancellors in twelve months: Bruning (until May 1932), Papen (June 1932), Schleicher (December 1932), Hitler (January 1933). Each was appointed by Hindenburg using Article 48; none commanded a Reichstag majority. By January 1933 parliamentary government had effectively ceased to function.

Papen's Cabinet of Barons, June 1932

In May 1932 Schleicher persuaded Hindenburg to dismiss Bruning and appoint Franz von Papen, an obscure Centre Party aristocrat with no Reichstag seat. Papen's cabinet was nicknamed the ‘Cabinet of Barons’ because nine of its eleven members were aristocrats. It had almost no support in the Reichstag — in a vote of confidence in September 1932, Papen lost 512 to 42.

Papen's most aggressive move was the ‘Preussenschlag’ of 20 July 1932 — he used Article 48 to dismiss the elected SPD-led Prussian state government and install himself as Reich Commissioner. This destroyed the largest democratic stronghold in Germany and removed an SPD-controlled police force that had been resisting Nazi street violence. Many historians see this as the decisive moment when Weimar democracy stopped defending itself.

In the July 1932 election the Nazis polled 37.4% and won 230 Reichstag seats — their high water mark. Hitler demanded the chancellorship. Hindenburg refused, telling Hitler to his face on 13 August 1932 that he would not appoint him to a presidential cabinet. Papen called fresh elections for November. The Nazi vote fell to 33.1% and 196 seats — a loss of 34 deputies and around two million votes. Communist support rose. Goebbels's diary recorded that party morale was collapsing and finances were near bankruptcy. If parliamentary politics had simply continued, the Nazi tide might have ebbed. It did not get the chance.

Schleicher's Failed Chancellorship, December 1932

In December 1932 Schleicher persuaded Hindenburg that he, rather than Papen, should now be Chancellor. Schleicher tried to build a ‘cross-front’ coalition by splitting Gregor Strasser's left wing of the Nazi Party away from Hitler and combining it with trade-union support. The strategy failed within four weeks. Strasser was politically broken; Schleicher had no Reichstag majority either; and the trade unions had no reason to trust an aristocratic general.

Meanwhile Papen, furious at being pushed out, was working in private to bring Hitler back into government — with himself as Vice-Chancellor pulling the strings. On 4 January 1933 Papen met Hitler in secret at the Cologne home of the banker Kurt von Schroeder. Industrial donors were lined up to pay off Nazi debts. Within three weeks Schleicher was finished.

The Appointment, 30 January 1933

On 28 January Schleicher resigned. On 29 January Papen presented Hindenburg with his proposed cabinet: Hitler as Chancellor, Papen as Vice-Chancellor and Reich Commissioner for Prussia, Alfred Hugenberg (DNVP) as Economics Minister, and only two other Nazis (Frick and Goring) in the cabinet of eleven. Papen reassured Hindenburg that they had ‘hired’ Hitler and could box him in: ‘Within two months we will have pushed Hitler so far into a corner that he'll squeak.’

Hindenburg, now 85, reluctantly agreed. At noon on 30 January 1933 Hitler was sworn in as Chancellor of Germany. That evening, lit torchlight columns of SA paraded through the Brandenburg Gate. Goebbels wrote in his diary: ‘It is almost like a dream. The Wilhelmstrasse is ours.’ The Nazi share of the cabinet was small — three of eleven — but Hitler had what mattered: control of the Chancellery, command of Reich-level policy, and a President willing to issue Article 48 decrees on his recommendation.

Three layers of cause are usually identified. Structural causes include the Treaty of Versailles, the Article 48 emergency provision, the use of proportional representation that produced fragmented Reichstags, and the survival of anti-democratic elites in the army, judiciary and civil service. Long-term causes include the Depression, the rise of the Nazi and Communist parties, and the discrediting of moderate parties by 1932. Contingent causes are the personal decisions of a small group: Hindenburg's willingness to govern by decree, Papen's vendetta against Schleicher, and the Cologne meeting of 4 January 1933. Hitler's appointment was not inevitable — it was the product of all three layers and an avoidable miscalculation by elite conservatives.

Key Fact

Hitler was appointed, not elected. The Nazis lost 34 seats in November 1932. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 because Papen persuaded Hindenburg that a Hitler-led cabinet of three Nazis and eight conservatives could be controlled. Papen's prediction — that they would push Hitler ‘into a corner’ within two months — was the most catastrophic miscalculation in twentieth-century European politics.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Three trip-wires for this lesson. First, never write ‘Hitler was elected Chancellor’ — he was appointed by Hindenburg on 30 January 1933, and the Nazi vote had actually fallen the previous November. Second, do not present the appointment as inevitable; it was the product of elite miscalculation, especially Papen's. Third, on 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation questions, watch for sources that single out either Hitler's appeal or backstairs intrigue alone — the strongest answers integrate both alongside the structural collapse of Weimar democracy under Article 48 rule. Lock in the four-chancellor sequence (Bruning, Papen, Schleicher, Hitler) and the cabinet ratio of 30 January 1933 (3 Nazis, 8 conservatives).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Weimar government had broken down before Hitler took power: four chancellors in twelve months, all governing by Article 48 emergency decree without a Reichstag majority.
  • The Nazi vote peaked at 37.4% in July 1932 and fell to 33.1% by November 1932 — Hitler's appointment was driven by elite intrigue, not by a rising electoral tide.
  • The decisive cause was Papen's Cologne deal of 4 January 1933 and Hindenburg's reluctant agreement to a cabinet of three Nazis and eight conservatives, in the catastrophic belief that Hitler could be controlled.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1933 article by Franz von Papen claiming the new cabinet would ‘tame’ Hitler within months) and Interpretation B (a 1948 memoir by an SPD politician arguing that Papen's deal made Nazi dictatorship inevitable) on Hitler's appointment as Chancellor. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the appointment as a controlled conservative manoeuvre — Hitler was outnumbered eight-to-three in cabinet and would be boxed in by Papen as Vice-Chancellor.
• Interpretation B presents the appointment as the moment Weimar democracy was lost — Papen had handed dictatorial machinery to a man with no respect for it.
• Main difference: A frames the deal as containment; B frames it as catastrophic miscalculation.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1933 Papen article) and Interpretation B (a 1948 SPD memoir) give different views about Hitler's appointment as Chancellor.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written at different times — Papen in 1933 had to defend his role to a conservative readership; the SPD writer in 1948 had seen the consequences of Nazi rule and the Holocaust.
• They had different purposes — Papen aimed to reassure conservative elites that the Nazis were under control; the SPD memoir aimed to apportion historical blame.
• They had access to different evidence — the 1948 writer knew about the Enabling Act, the camps and the war; Papen at the time of writing did not.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in January 1933 was the inevitable result of the Nazi Party's electoral success during the Depression.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about how Hitler became Chancellor?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Nazis were the largest Reichstag party from July 1932 with 230 seats — no government could be formed without acknowledging them.
• Convincing because Hindenburg's circle saw harnessing the Nazi vote as the only way to govern without the SPD.
• Less convincing because the Nazi vote fell from 37.4% to 33.1% between July and November 1932 — the surge was already ebbing.
• Less convincing because the appointment was the product of personal deals, not electoral logic — the Cologne meeting of 4 January 1933 between Papen and Hitler was decisive.
• Less convincing because Hindenburg had refused Hitler the chancellorship as recently as 13 August 1932; only Papen's intervention changed that.
• Overall judgement: the Depression and Nazi vote share created the conditions, but the specific appointment was the product of elite miscalculation rather than electoral inevitability. Historiographically, Sonderweg arguments stress structural inevitability while contingency-focused historians stress the avoidable choices of January 1933.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Papen's chancellorship (June–December 1932) on the political crisis that led to Hitler's appointment.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Preussenschlag of 20 July 1932 dismissed the elected SPD-led Prussian government and removed the largest democratic stronghold in Germany — a major step in the breakdown of Weimar self-defence.
• Papen's lack of Reichstag support (he lost a confidence vote 512 to 42 in September 1932) entrenched government by Article 48 decree and discredited parliamentary politics still further.
• The November 1932 election he called produced a Nazi loss — but also showed no stable majority was available to anyone, deepening the appearance that only authoritarian rule could work.
• After his dismissal in December, Papen's resentment of Schleicher led to the Cologne meeting of 4 January 1933 with Hitler, the deal that put Hitler in the Chancellery on 30 January 1933.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933.
You may consider:
• the role of the Depression and the Nazi vote share
• the role of Papen, Hindenburg and Schleicher.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Depression and Nazi growth: industrial output fell 40% (1929–32); six million unemployed; Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (1928) to 37.4% (July 1932), making them the largest Reichstag party.
• Hindenburg's reluctance: refused Hitler the chancellorship on 13 August 1932; called him ‘the Bohemian corporal’; appointed Bruning, Papen, Schleicher in turn.
• Papen's role: Cabinet of Barons (June 1932); Preussenschlag dismissing Prussian SPD government (July 1932); Cologne meeting with Hitler (4 January 1933); served as Vice-Chancellor in cabinet of three Nazis and eight conservatives.

• Limits of inevitability: Nazi vote had fallen by November 1932 to 196 seats; party finances near bankruptcy; without Papen's intervention Hitler might never have been appointed.
• Conclusion: the Depression and Nazi vote share created the political space; structural collapse of Weimar parliamentary government under Article 48 deepened it; but the specific appointment was driven by Papen's vendetta against Schleicher and Hindenburg's catastrophic acceptance of the ‘hired’ Hitler argument.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1990s biographer arguing Hindenburg's age and conservative advisers were decisive in Hitler's appointment) and Interpretation B (a 2000s structural historian arguing Weimar democracy was already dead before January 1933) on the failure of Weimar democracy. Students may include:

lessons.title: Hitler's dictatorship — Reichstag Fire to Fuhrer
lessons.description: From the Reichstag flames to the Night of the Long Knives — 18 months to total power.
lessons.content_html:
When Hitler took office on 30 January 1933 he had a cabinet of three Nazis among eight conservatives, no Reichstag majority, and a Vice-Chancellor (Papen) who believed he had ‘hired’ him. Eighteen months later he was Fuhrer, the SA was decapitated, the army had sworn a personal oath of loyalty to him, and every other political party was illegal. This lesson tracks how Hitler turned the Chancellery into a dictatorship between 30 January 1933 and 2 August 1934 — using legal forms, manufactured emergencies and one weekend of state murder.

The Reichstag Fire, 27 February 1933

A month after Hitler's appointment, the Reichstag building burned down. A young Dutch communist, Marinus van der Lubbe, was found at the scene with matches and firelighters. Most current historians accept he acted alone, but the Nazis exploited the fire as if it were the start of a Communist uprising. The next morning, 28 February, Hindenburg signed the Decree for the Protection of the People and State. It suspended freedom of speech, assembly and the press, allowed unlimited detention without trial, and permitted the central government to take over state powers. Roughly 4,000 KPD activists were arrested in the first wave.

The decree was passed using Article 48 of the Weimar constitution — the same emergency provision Hindenburg had used to govern Germany since 1930. Once signed, it was never repealed. The legal foundation of the Third Reich was a single emergency decree justified by a single act of arson.

Key Fact

The Reichstag Fire of 27 February 1933 was probably the work of a lone Communist, Marinus van der Lubbe. The Nazis used it to justify the Decree for the Protection of the People and State on 28 February. That decree suspended civil liberties for the entire life of the regime — it was never repealed.

The March 1933 Election and the Enabling Act

A new Reichstag election had already been called for 5 March 1933. With KPD candidates in jail and SA squads breaking up SPD meetings, the Nazis still won only 43.9% of the vote — not the majority Hitler had wanted. With the DNVP's 8.0% on top, however, he had a working coalition. The new task was the Enabling Act: a constitutional amendment letting the cabinet pass laws without the Reichstag or the President for four years. Because it changed the constitution, it required a two-thirds majority.

On 23 March 1933, in the Kroll Opera House (the Reichstag was still ruined), the Act was put to the vote. The KPD's 81 deputies were already in jail or fled. The Centre Party was bargained into voting yes by Hitler's vague promise to protect Catholic schools. Only the SPD's 94 deputies voted against. The final vote was 444 in favour, 94 against. Hitler now ruled by decree on the cabinet's signature alone — legally, with the Reichstag's own consent.

The Act was a constitutional amendment with five articles. The crucial one was Article 2, which let the Reich government pass laws that ‘deviated from the constitution’. Within four months it had been used to outlaw trade unions (2 May 1933), ban the SPD (22 June), and dissolve all other political parties (14 July, declared a one-party state). It was renewed in 1937 and 1939 and remained in force until 1945. The Enabling Act made Hitler a legal dictator. It did not make him Fuhrer — that came in August 1934.

Gleichschaltung — Bringing Germany Into Line

From spring 1933 the Nazis pursued Gleichschaltung — literally ‘coordination’ or ‘bringing into line’. Federal state governments were placed under Reich Commissioners (April). Trade unions were broken on 2 May 1933 — the day after Labour Day rallies, the SA stormed union offices and arrested leaders. Their assets were transferred to a new state body, the German Labour Front (DAF), under Robert Ley. Strikes were illegal. Wages were set by Reich Trustees of Labour.

In June and July 1933 the SPD was banned and the remaining parties dissolved themselves. On 14 July 1933 a Law Against the Formation of Parties declared the NSDAP the only legal party in Germany. The civil service was purged of Jews and political opponents under the Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service (April 1933). Within six months Germany had a one-party state, no independent unions and a politicised bureaucracy — all without overturning the formal constitution.

The Night of the Long Knives, 30 June 1934

By 1934 Hitler faced one remaining problem inside the Nazi movement itself. The SA, now four million strong under Ernst Rohm, wanted a ‘second revolution’. Rohm wanted the SA to absorb the Reichswehr (army) and become a true revolutionary force. The Reichswehr generals refused to be subordinated to street-fighting brownshirts. With Hindenburg dying, Hitler had to choose between the army and the SA — and he chose the army.

Between 30 June and 2 July 1934 the SS, on Hitler's orders, murdered the SA leadership. Rohm was shot in his cell at Stadelheim Prison. At least 85 people were killed; some estimates run to 200. Old enemies were settled along the way: Schleicher and his wife were shot at home; the Catholic conservative leader Erich Klausener was murdered in his office; Strasser was killed in Gestapo custody. On 13 July 1934 Hitler defended the killings to the Reichstag, calling himself ‘the supreme judge of the German people’. The SA was reduced to a propaganda formation; the SS rose under Himmler.

The Reichswehr leaders had a deal. Defence Minister Werner von Blomberg had agreed in spring 1934 that if Hitler removed the SA threat, the army would back him as Hindenburg's successor. The purge delivered on this. Within five weeks Hindenburg was dead and the army swore the Hitler Oath of personal loyalty to the Fuhrer in person. The Reichswehr had bought Hitler's protection from the SA at the price of its own independence as a state institution.

Hindenburg Dies; Hitler Becomes Fuhrer

On 2 August 1934 President Hindenburg died, aged 86. Within hours Hitler announced that the offices of Chancellor and President would be merged. He took the new title Fuhrer — head of state, head of government and commander-in-chief in one person. The same day every officer and soldier of the Reichswehr swore a personal oath of loyalty — not to the constitution, not to Germany, but to Hitler personally. A 19 August plebiscite endorsed the merger of offices with 88% of the vote.

Eighteen months after his appointment Hitler had used law (the Reichstag Fire Decree, the Enabling Act), state violence (the SA purge) and contingency (Hindenburg's death) to turn a coalition Chancellor of three Nazis among eleven into the unchallenged dictator of a one-party state. The Weimar constitution was technically still in force. In practice it had ceased to exist.

Key Fact

The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 made Hitler a legal dictator. The Night of the Long Knives of 30 June 1934 destroyed the SA threat and bought army loyalty. The death of Hindenburg on 2 August 1934 let Hitler merge the offices of Chancellor and President, taking the title Fuhrer. Three different acts — do not confuse them.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Two precision points. First, do not write that the Enabling Act made Hitler Fuhrer — the Enabling Act made him a legal dictator on 23 March 1933; the Fuhrer title came after Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934. Second, do not say the Nazis started the Reichstag Fire — that was once a popular theory but most current historians accept van der Lubbe acted alone. The Nazis exploited the fire; they did not light it. For 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation questions, watch for sources that overstate Nazi planning — the regime improvised, especially after the Fire and Hindenburg's death. Lock in the four key dates: 27 February 1933, 23 March 1933, 30 June 1934, 2 August 1934.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933 suspended civil liberties for the life of the regime; the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 let Hitler's cabinet legislate without the Reichstag or the President.
  • Gleichschaltung between April and July 1933 broke the trade unions, banned the SPD, dissolved every other party and turned Germany into a one-party state — without overturning the formal Weimar constitution.
  • The Night of the Long Knives (30 June 1934) destroyed the SA threat in exchange for army loyalty; Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934 let Hitler merge Chancellor and President into the title Fuhrer.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1934 Goebbels speech presenting the Night of the Long Knives as Hitler's defence of the German people from a treacherous SA conspiracy) and Interpretation B (a post-war study arguing the purge was a calculated bargain with the army to secure Hitler's succession to Hindenburg) on the Night of the Long Knives. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the killings as a defensive emergency — Hitler acted as ‘supreme judge’ against an SA plot to overthrow the state.
• Interpretation B presents the killings as a deliberate political deal — Hitler removed the SA in exchange for army loyalty after Hindenburg's death.
• Main difference: A frames the purge as defensive crisis-management; B frames it as a calculated transaction.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1934 Goebbels speech) and Interpretation B (a post-war academic study) give different views about the Night of the Long Knives.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — Goebbels in 1934 needed to justify state murder to a German public; the post-war historian aimed to explain the consolidation of dictatorship.
• They had access to different evidence — the historian could use the Hitler Oath of 2 August 1934 and Reichswehr archives; Goebbels could not refer to the army's deal openly.
• They were written in different political conditions — Goebbels under regime censorship; the historian after free access to documents.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Enabling Act of March 1933 was the moment Weimar democracy ended.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the establishment of Hitler's dictatorship?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Enabling Act gave the cabinet power to pass laws without the Reichstag or the President for four years — the legal foundation of dictatorship.
• Convincing because within four months it was used to ban trade unions (2 May), the SPD (22 June) and all other parties (14 July).
• Less convincing because the Decree for the Protection of the People and State (28 February 1933) had already suspended civil liberties — democracy was effectively over before 23 March.
• Less convincing because the Hitler Oath and Fuhrer title only came on 2 August 1934 — the army's independence as an institution was not subordinated until then.
• Less convincing because Weimar democracy had been governed by Article 48 since March 1930 — some structural historians argue parliamentary government had ended even before Hitler's appointment.
• Overall judgement: the Enabling Act was the decisive legal step but the breakdown was a process running from March 1930 to August 1934, not a single moment.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Reichstag Fire of 27 February 1933 on Hitler's establishment of his dictatorship.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It triggered the Decree for the Protection of the People and State on 28 February 1933 — suspending civil liberties and allowing detention without trial; never repealed.
• Around 4,000 KPD activists were arrested, neutralising the largest opposition party before the 5 March election.
• It contributed to the Nazi vote of 43.9% in March 1933 — with the DNVP's 8.0%, gave Hitler a working coalition for the Enabling Act.
• It enabled the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 — with the KPD removed and the Centre Party bargained over Catholic schools, the two-thirds majority for constitutional amendment was achievable.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how Hitler turned the Chancellorship into a personal dictatorship between January 1933 and August 1934.
You may consider:
• the use of legal instruments (Reichstag Fire Decree, Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung)
• the use of state violence (Night of the Long Knives) and the death of Hindenburg.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Legal route: Reichstag Fire Decree (28 Feb 1933) suspended civil liberties; Enabling Act (23 Mar 1933) let cabinet legislate alone; banning of trade unions (2 May), SPD (22 Jun), all parties (14 Jul); civil service purge under April 1933 law.
• Gleichschaltung: federal states placed under Reich Commissioners; DAF replaced unions; one-party state declared 14 July 1933.
• State violence: Night of the Long Knives, 30 June 1934 — Rohm and at least 85 SA leaders murdered; Schleicher, Klausener and Strasser also killed; SA neutralised.
• Army deal: Blomberg's spring 1934 agreement — remove the SA threat in exchange for army support as Hindenburg's successor; Hitler Oath of 2 August 1934 sworn to Hitler personally.
• Contingency: Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934 allowed merger of Chancellor and President; 19 August plebiscite endorsed it with 88%.
• Conclusion: legal instruments built the framework, the Night of the Long Knives bought the army's loyalty, and Hindenburg's death allowed the consolidation. None alone would have been enough — together they took eighteen months to turn a coalition Chancellor into Fuhrer.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1980s functionalist historian arguing that Nazi consolidation was an improvised process driven by events such as the Reichstag Fire) and Interpretation B (a 1990s intentionalist historian arguing that Hitler followed a clear plan to dismantle democracy from January 1933) on the establishment of Hitler's dictatorship. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A frames consolidation as opportunistic — the Reichstag Fire and Hindenburg's death were exploited rather than planned.
• Interpretation B frames consolidation as the execution of a long-held plan — the Enabling Act, Gleichschaltung and the SA purge were all foreseeable steps.
• Main difference: A emphasises improvisation and contingency; B emphasises planning and intent.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

lessons.title: The Nazi economy — work, rearmament and self-sufficiency
lessons.description: Public works, the Four Year Plan and the price of guns over butter for ordinary Germans.
lessons.content_html:
When Hitler took power in January 1933 there were six million unemployed Germans. By 1939 official unemployment was under 200,000. Nazi propaganda presented this as a miracle. The reality was more complicated: the figures depended on who was counted, work creation was largely a side-effect of rearmament, and consumers paid for the recovery in lower wages, longer hours and shortages of basic goods. This lesson tracks the Nazi economy from Schacht's New Plan in 1934 to the Four Year Plan of 1936 and the choices behind the slogan ‘guns or butter’.

Schacht's New Plan, 1934

The first phase of recovery was managed by Hjalmar Schacht, a conservative banker who had helped end the 1923 hyperinflation. Schacht became Reichsbank President in March 1933 and Economics Minister in August 1934. His New Plan tackled three problems at once: shortage of foreign exchange, dependence on imports, and mass unemployment.

Schacht imposed strict import controls and signed bilateral trade agreements with Balkan states (Yugoslavia, Romania, Bulgaria), paying for raw materials in blocked Reichsmarks rather than hard currency. He used Mefo bills — promissory notes issued by a shell company — to disguise the true scale of military spending. By 1936 unemployment was down to one million. But Schacht warned Hitler that rearmament was now outrunning what the economy could support without inflation. Hitler was unimpressed.

Key Fact

Official German unemployment fell from six million in 1933 to one million by 1936 and under 200,000 by 1939. The figures are flattering: Jews dismissed under the April 1933 civil service law, women pushed out of professions, political prisoners and the 1.4 million conscripted from 1935 were all redefined out of the count.

Public Works and the Reich Labour Service

Job creation began before Hitler took power, but the Nazis claimed credit and expanded it. The most visible programme was the autobahn network: 7,000 kilometres planned, 3,000 km completed by 1938. Around 125,000 men worked on autobahn construction at peak. Other programmes included public housing, draining marshes, planting forests and building government offices.

From 1935 the RAD (Reichsarbeitsdienst) made six months of labour service compulsory for young men aged 18–25. It paid pocket money rather than a wage, lived under quasi-military discipline, and worked on agricultural drainage, road-building and forestry. From 1939 it was extended to women too. The RAD was a labour scheme, a propaganda spectacle and a pre-conscription training pipeline rolled into one.

In March 1935 Hitler announced conscription in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles, raising the army from 100,000 to 550,000 by 1936. Conscription alone removed roughly 1.4 million young men from the unemployment count. Rearmament also pulled steel, chemicals, coal and engineering firms back into mass production: military spending rose from 1% of GDP in 1933 to around 18% by 1938. Krupp, Thyssen and IG Farben all expanded sharply. The recovery was real for these firms; for consumers it meant their resources were diverted to weapons. The historiographical debate over whether the Nazis ‘solved’ unemployment turns on whether you count conscripts and dismissed Jews and women as employed, unemployed, or simply absent from the figures.

The Four Year Plan, 1936

In August 1936 Hitler issued a secret memorandum demanding that ‘the German army must be operational and the German economy fit for war within four years’. He put Hermann Goring — not Schacht — in charge of a new Four Year Plan. The aim was autarky: economic self-sufficiency that would let Germany fight a war without depending on imports.

The Plan poured investment into synthetic substitutes — synthetic oil from coal, synthetic rubber (Buna), artificial textiles. New plants were built at Leuna and Schkopau. Steel production was forced through new plants at Salzgitter (the Hermann Goring Werke). Imports of consumer goods were squeezed. By 1939 Germany still imported a third of its raw materials. Autarky was a goal, not a reality. But arms production rose sharply: by 1939 Germany was producing 8,000 aircraft a year. Schacht resigned as Economics Minister in November 1937, warning Hitler that the country was running out of foreign exchange.

Strength Through Joy and Beauty of Labour

For workers, the Nazis offered carrots as well as sticks. The German Labour Front (DAF) under Robert Ley ran two flagship organisations. Strength Through Joy (KdF) offered cheap holidays, theatre trips, sports events and concerts. By 1938 ten million Germans had taken a KdF holiday — mostly day trips, but cruises to Madeira and Norway also ran. Beauty of Labour (SdA) improved factory canteens, washrooms and lighting.

The famous KdF promise was the Volkswagen — the ‘people's car’ that workers could buy through a savings scheme launched in 1938. Roughly 336,000 Germans paid in. Not one civilian Volkswagen was delivered before 1945; the factory was switched to making the Kubelwagen for the army. Like much of Nazi welfare, KdF combined real benefits, real propaganda value and an undertow of state fraud.

Drawbacks for Workers and Consumers

Behind the propaganda, ordinary German workers paid in three currencies. First, real wages fell or stagnated for most of the 1930s — not until 1938 did average industrial wages match 1928 levels. The DAF set wages; strikes were illegal; workbooks restricted job changes from 1935. Second, the working week lengthened — from 43 hours in 1933 to over 49 by 1939, with bonus pay for overtime gradually eroded. Third, consumer goods were rationed in all but name — meat, butter, dairy and textiles were all in short supply by 1939 because resources had gone into arms.

Goring put the choice plainly in 1936: ‘Guns will make us powerful; butter will only make us fat.’ The Nazi economy delivered on guns. It did not deliver on butter.

Two competing answers. The official answer is yes — six million in 1933 to under 200,000 in 1939. The qualified answer is partial — subtract roughly 1.4 million conscripts, perhaps half a million Jews dismissed under the April 1933 law, women redefined out of full-time work, and political prisoners in the camps, and the figure of true productive employment is much smaller. Historians of the Nazi economy (Tooze; Overy) generally accept the recovery was real but driven by rearmament rather than productive demand — an ‘armaments boom’ that could only end in war or collapse.

Key Fact

By 1938 around 18% of German GDP went to the military, up from 1% in 1933. Average industrial wages did not match 1928 levels until 1938, the working week stretched to over 49 hours, and consumer goods were rationed in all but name. The economy worked — for armaments. It did not work for consumers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Three precision points. First, do not write that the Nazis ‘solved unemployment’ without qualification — conscription, sackings of Jews and women, and prison labour all flatter the figures. Second, do not credit the autobahns as the main jobs programme — rearmament and conscription mattered more from 1935. Third, do not assume real wages rose in the 1930s — for most workers they fell or stagnated. For 8-mark Explain Effects questions, link the policy (Four Year Plan, RAD, KdF) to specific groups (industrialists, young men, workers, consumers) rather than ‘the German people’ in general.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Schacht's New Plan (1934) and the Four Year Plan (1936) drove unemployment from six million to under 200,000 by 1939 — mostly through public works, conscription and rearmament rather than productive consumer demand.
  • Autarky was the goal of the Four Year Plan but was never achieved — Germany still imported a third of raw materials in 1939; the New Plan and Mefo bills disguised a deepening foreign-exchange crisis.
  • Workers gained jobs and KdF leisure but lost free unions, real-wage growth and consumer choice — Goring's choice of ‘guns over butter’ defines the trade-off behind the recovery.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1937 Nazi propaganda film celebrating the autobahns and KdF holidays as proof of national renewal) and Interpretation B (a modern study of German real wages arguing that workers funded the rearmament boom through stagnant pay and longer hours) on the Nazi economy. Students may include:

Students may include:

• They drew on different evidence — the film used selected sites and individuals; the modern study used wage indices, working-hours data and household budgets.
• They were produced under different conditions — the 1937 film under regime censorship and propaganda direction; the modern study with full archival access.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Nazi recovery between 1933 and 1939 made ordinary Germans materially better off.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the impact of Nazi economic policy on workers and consumers?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because unemployment fell from six million in 1933 to under 200,000 in 1939 — jobs were a real material gain.
• Convincing because KdF gave 10 million Germans a holiday by 1938; Beauty of Labour improved canteens and washrooms.
• Less convincing because real wages did not match 1928 levels until 1938; the working week rose to over 49 hours by 1939.
• Less convincing because consumer goods (meat, butter, textiles) were rationed in all but name as resources went to rearmament.
• Less convincing because workers lost trade unions and the right to strike; workbooks from 1935 restricted job movement; women and Jews were redefined out of work.
• Overall judgement: jobs were a real gain, but pay, hours, choice and freedom were lost — the answer depends on which group of workers and which year you choose.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

• Military spending rose from around 10% of GDP in 1936 to roughly 18% by 1938; aircraft production reached around 8,000 per year by 1939.
• Consumer goods squeezed — meat, butter and textile shortages by 1939; foreign-exchange crisis deepened, prompting Schacht's resignation as Economics Minister in November 1937.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

Construct an explanation of how Nazi economic policy between 1933 and 1939 affected different groups in German society.
You may consider:
• the impact on industrialists and the unemployed
• the impact on workers and consumers.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Industrialists: Krupp, Thyssen, IG Farben and the Hermann Goring Werke benefited from rearmament orders; cartels protected from foreign competition; trade-union threat removed.
• Unemployed: official unemployment fell from six million (1933) to under 200,000 (1939); RAD and conscription absorbed young men; autobahn programme employed roughly 125,000.
• Workers: jobs and KdF leisure programmes (10m holidays by 1938); but no unions, no strikes, real wages flat until 1938, working week up to 49 hours, workbooks from 1935.
• Consumers: shortages of meat, butter and textiles by 1939; Volkswagen savings scheme paid in by 336,000 with no civilian cars delivered before 1945.
• Excluded groups: Jews dismissed from civil service (April 1933); women squeezed out of professions; conscripts removed from civilian work.
• Conclusion: industrialists and the previously unemployed gained substantially; workers gained jobs but lost wage freedom; consumers funded the rearmament boom through shortages and inflation suppressed by price controls. The recovery was real but unevenly shared, and depended on a permanent expansion of military spending.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]
